text: Practice makes perfect.
Better late than never.
Actions speak louder than words.
Every cloud has a silver lining.
Time flies when you are busy.
Look before you leap.
Two heads are better than one.
A good start is half the work.
A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step.
The early bird catches the worm, but the second mouse gets the cheese.
You never really know a puzzle until you have solved it twice.
Small daily habits quietly build the biggest changes.
A clear question is already half of a good answer.
Patience turns a hard problem into a series of easy ones.
Read the whole page before you decide what it means.
Good ideas often arrive while you are doing something else.
A careful observer notices the pattern where a hurried one sees nothing but random noise.
Experienced players evaluate the whole position before calculating any particular variation.
The real difficulty of a puzzle rarely lies in its size but in the obscurity of the first move.
Doubting your own conclusions is the cheapest insurance against expensive mistakes.
Every deciphered letter narrows the possibilities and accelerates the remaining search.
Memory keeps what you understood far longer than what you merely repeated.
Logic without imagination is sterile, and imagination without logic is helpless.
Curiosity drags the researcher back to problems that everyone else abandoned long ago.
A cryptographer, studying symbol frequencies, gradually exposes the hidden structure of a message; patience matters more than erudition or a lucky guess.
Paradoxically, simplifying an explanation frequently demands considerably more effort than complicating it ever would.
Heuristics is the craft of finding an acceptable answer when an exhaustive search is, by any reasonable estimate, impossible.
The scrupulous analyst records even the most trivial anomalies: afterwards, they quite often turn out to be the key.
Overconfident players neglect to verify hypotheses, and they pay for it by having to begin the whole analysis again.
A grandmaster's phenomenal intuition is not mysticism but the experience of thousands of games, squeezed into an instant.
Whoever judges a jigsaw by its box quickly discovers that the awkward, unexceptional pieces determine everything.
Mnemonic techniques work because vivid, exaggerated images outlive dry and perfectly sensible facts.
